tone_statements.quote: This paper presents the Ngie (spoken in the Grasslands area of Cameroon) noun classes and tone system. Most Ngie nouns have a V,-C,(G)V,(C,) shape. The first vowel (i.e. the prefix) can either be i-, a-, or u- and can have either low or mid tone. The second vowel can have one of the following six tone shapes: low with downgliding before pause L [—_], low level L° [ —_], mid level [ —], high H [~ J], falling F [ ~] and rising R [ _~]. Out of the twelve theoretical tonal combinations, only two patterns are lacking: mid followed by level low and mid followed by rising tone. Comparison with Proto-Bantu reconstructions suggest the following corre- spondences: a) L-L, L-F and M-F Ngie tone classes correspond to an earlier L-LL sequence; b) L-L? and M-M Ngie tone classes correspond to an earlier L-LH sequence; c) L~M and M-H in Ngie correspond to an earlier L-HL sequence. The most likely historical scenario for these developments seems to be the following: a) all prefixes were low; b) in certain contexts, the tone of the prefix was changed from low to mid except in cases in which the prefix was followed by a NC consonant cluster; c) nasals were lost when followed by a voiceless segment a…
tone_statements.translation: (scanned of a 1977 typescript: 'V,-C,(G)V,(C,)' = V1-C1(G)V2(C2) with subscript indices; 'L°' = level low L with ring diacritic; 'L-L?' = L-Llevel; 'L~M' = L-M; the bracketed pitch glyphs after each tone name are hand-drawn contour marks rendered as ASCII by scanned.)

tone_statements.summary: Lexical tone language. Nouns V1-C1(G)V2(C2): prefix vowel L or M; stem syllable one of six surface tones/contours (falling-to-pause L, level L, M, H, HL fall, LH rise); 10 attested prefix+stem tone classes; M prefixes arose historically from L except before NC clusters (nasal depressor effect); tone classes map onto Proto-Bantu *L-LL, *L-LH, *L-HL.

sources.citation: Watters, John R. 1990. Reduplication and the origin of high tone on noun prefixes in Ejagham. Journal of West African Languages 20(1): 105-117.
sources.note: Section 3 (p. 107) 'Non-low tone noun prefixes in Ngie and Narrow Grassfields' summarises Hombert 1976 (Ngie non-low prefix tones derive from a high-toned preprefix); the only 'stress' mention is Hyman's diachronic Proto-Ring hypothesis ('Low tone prefixes would derive from high tone prefixes through loss of stem stress'). Nothing on synchronic Ngie word stress; secondary for Ngie.

sources.note: States the Ngie noun tone system: prefixes i-/a-/u- carry L or M tone; the stem vowel carries one of six surface tone shapes (L with pre-pausal downglide, level L, M, H, falling, rising); of the 12 prefix x stem combinations only M+level-L and M+rising are missing; gives Proto-Bantu correspondences (Ngie L-L, L-F, M-F < *L-LL; L-Llevel, M-M < *L-LH; L-M, M-H < *L-HL) and a history in which all prefixes were L and were raised to M except before NC clusters.
